passage: Binita, you keep calling yourself "metal mouth" before anyone else can? Let me tell you your Tenzin Uncle's story. At fifteen, in Darjeeling, I got braces and thick glasses in the same month. On the first day back, before anyone could say a word, I stood up and announced, "Behold, the robot has arrived!" Everyone laughed. It worked. They liked me. So I kept doing it: my glasses, my marks, my skinny legs. I was always first with the joke. But by the end of the year, the boys had started making the jokes for me, and they weren't funny any more. One of them called me "Robot" until we finished school. I had taught them where to aim. Laugh at yourself sometimes, it's healthy. Just don't hand them the script every day.

qa.q: What did Tenzin announce on the first day back?
qa.a: "Behold, the robot has arrived!"

qa.q: Why did Tenzin keep being first with the joke?
qa.a: Getting the laugh first felt safe and won acceptance, so he didn't have to wait nervously for others to tease him.

qa.q: What choice is Tenzin Uncle hoping Binita will make about the 'metal mouth' jokes?
qa.a: To keep a light joke now and then but stop leading with it every day, so the others don't learn where to aim.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling as Uncle tells the story?
qa.a: Binita might feel caught out but also understood, since Uncle clearly knows why the 'metal mouth' jokes feel safer.

grounding: An uncle tells how, as a teenager, mocking his own braces and glasses first won laughs but taught others to treat him as a target.

passage:
The maths results were being read aloud, one name at a time, and Vishal knew his was bad. Worse, he had moved to this school only two weeks earlier and knew almost no one. When Sir said, "Vishal: thirty-one," Vishal leaned back and said, "Thirty-one! My highest score ever! Someone call my parents!" The class laughed, and a boy clapped him on the back. At lunch his new classmate Usha offered him half her paratha.
By Friday, Vishal was joking about his handwriting, his accent from his old city, his skinny arms. Everyone laughed each time. But on Saturday, when a boy called him "Thirty-one" in the corridor and others joined in, Vishal didn't find it funny at all, and he had no joke left to make.

qa.q: What mark did Sir read out for Vishal?
qa.a: Thirty-one.

qa.q: Why did joking about his own mark feel like the right move to Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal was nervous about being mocked as the new boy with a bad mark, so laughing first let him look relaxed and win friends before anyone else could.

qa.q: What could Vishal try the next time he feels the urge to joke about himself?
qa.a: Keep the odd light joke, but sometimes just shrug or say 'I'll do better next time', so classmates don't learn to see him as the target.

qa.q: How might Usha see the 'Thirty-one' nickname in the corridor?
qa.a: Usha might realise the jokes Vishal started have turned against him, and could choose not to join in or even speak up for him.

grounding: A new boy mocks his own low marks before anyone else can, wins acceptance, and then finds the class using his jokes against him.

Irawati had her braces tightened on Friday, and on Monday at the bus stop in Dadar she smiled wide before anyone could look. "Welcome to the metal museum," she said. "Entry free, no photos." qa.q: What choice could Irawati make now that the joke has spread?

passage:
In Class 10 I had a joke for every test. When the maths papers came back, I'd hold mine up before anyone asked: "Nineteen! A personal best. Somebody call the news." People laughed. They liked me for it. It felt much better than waiting for someone to notice.
The trouble came slowly. By December, people started the joke for me. "Ask Payal, she'll know the wrong answer." When I got sixty-eight in the pre-boards, the boys at the back said, "Who did you copy from?" Nobody believed I could just get a good mark.
My best friend Indu was the one who said it. "Payal, you taught them that. You keep telling everyone you're stupid."
I'm in Class 11 now. I still make jokes, just not about my own brain. It's quieter. But when I got a good mark last week, people only said, "Nice."

qa.q: What did Payal say when she held up a nineteen?
qa.a: "Nineteen! A personal best. Somebody call the news."

qa.q: Why did joking first feel better to Payal than waiting?
qa.a: It let her control the moment and win laughs and liking, instead of dreading someone else noticing the low mark.

qa.q: What choice has Payal made since Indu spoke up?
qa.a: She still jokes, just not about her own brain, so classmates no longer treat her as the target and a good mark gets a simple "Nice."

qa.q: Why might the boys at the back ask "Who did you copy from?" after the sixty-eight?
qa.a: They had heard Payal call herself stupid so often that they believed it, so a good mark looked suspicious to them.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who mocked her own marks before anyone else could, winning acceptance until classmates began to see her as the target.

passage: Tejas, you asked why I've stopped joking about my braces. Okay, here's Charu's honest version. When I got them in class nine, I decided to get in first. Before anyone could say anything, I'd say, "Hi, I'm a walking fence," or, "Don't stand near me in a thunderstorm." Everyone laughed. It worked. People liked me. Nobody could hurt me with something I'd already said. But after a few months, it changed. People started saying the jokes to me. "Oi, metal mouth." "Fence girl." And they weren't laughing with me anymore. They'd learnt from me that my braces were fair game. That was the day I realised I'd taught them how to treat me. So now I just don't mention them. If someone does, I say, "Not funny," and change the subject.

qa.q: What joke did Charu make about the braces?
qa.a: "A walking fence."

qa.q: Why did Charu joke about the braces before anyone else could?
qa.a: Charu felt nervous and self-conscious, and joking first felt like protection, because nobody could hurt Charu with something already said.

qa.q: What did Charu change, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Charu stopped the self-mocking jokes and started saying "Not funny," which stops others treating the braces as fair game.

qa.q: How might classmates have started to see Charu over those months?
qa.a: Some classmates came to see Charu as an easy target, because the jokes had shown them the braces were open to mockery.

grounding: Shows a teenager mocking their own braces before anyone else could, winning acceptance but teaching others to treat them as a target.

passage: Tejas, you keep making jokes about your weight at school. Your Jatin mama wants to tell you something. When I was fifteen, in Mysuru, I had very big ears. I decided that if I joked first, nobody could hurt me. So on the first day of class ten, I said, "Don't worry, I can hear you from the back row. Built-in speakers." The class loved it. For a month I was the funny one. But then the jokes weren't mine anymore. Boys I didn't know called me "Dumbo" in the corridor. They flicked my ears. I had given them permission. One day, my friend Suresh said, "Stop it, Jatin. You're making yourself easy." That was the turning point. I stopped. When someone made a joke, I didn't laugh. It took a term. But it stopped.

In the queue, before anyone could look twice, she flashed a huge metal grin. "Don't stand too close, I pick up radio signals." The girls around her laughed, and Dilnaz, whom she'd met that morning, said, "You're funny!"

Then, in the afternoon, a boy she didn't know shouted across the corridor, "Oi, radio signals!" and his friends cackled. Binita laughed along. Dilnaz didn't. "He's using your joke on you," she said quietly.

Walking home, her friend Kalyani said, "You're not bad at maths. You just joke like you are. Now they joke first." Avni kicked a stone and didn't answer.

passage: When I got braces in Class 9, I decided to strike first. "Metal mouth reporting for duty!" I'd say before anyone else could. I called myself "tin can" and "robot jaws".
